articles.text: Edible Contest, Farmer’s Market, Food Trucks keep Piedmonters well-fed Last Sunday, September 24, Piedmont’s 25th Annual Harvest Festival drew the community to Piedmont Park with a variety of different activities and traditions in Piedmont Park. There was music, art, food, and laughter as families enjoyed the festivities on a day with perfect weather. There was plenty for adults – an Art Show at the Japanese Tea House, the annual Edibles Contest, and an exhibit on oak trees by the Piedmont Garden Club. Arguably there was just as much for kids between Scarecrow Alley and the fairground games at the kids’ carnival. If festival-goers got hungry, they could grab a bite at the Village Market’s fresh produce booth or at one of the many food trucks on the street bordering the park on-site. And at the end of the day, everyone could sit comfortably on the green to enjoy the sounds of the Piedmont Jazz Festival. All in all, it was a wonderful way to ring in a quarter-century of community building and family memories. Judges arrived at Piedmont Community Hall last Sunday starting at 7:30 a.m. to begin their deliberations of the best entries in the annual Harvest Festival’s Edible Food Contest. By 11 a.m. they made their decisions and opened the doors to the public. Judges were drawn largely from city public bodies, including City Council as well as several commissions and committees. From savory to sweet, this year’s Edibles Contest had a record number of entrants. Community members competed in categories like Best Apple Pie, Best Cake, Best Jam, Best Bars, Best Pesto, Biggest Squash, Biggest Pumpkin, Most Unusual Hungry customers line up at the food trucks at this year’s Harvest Festival. articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Jasdeep Singh was honored with the Life-Saving Medal by the Piedmont Police Department for actions that helped save a man’s life earlier this year. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers presented the medal at a City Council meeting on September 18. On the afternoon of April 25, Singh responded to a report of a man suffering a medical emergency at the corner of Grand Avenue and Jean Street on the Piedmont-Oakland border. When he arrived at the scene, Singh found the man lying on the ground and unresponsive. Singh immediately began performing CPR on the unconscious man and continued to do so for six minutes until the Oakland Fire Department arrived to take over care of the individual. EMS personnel continued care following Singh’s initial response and soon they established a pulse. The man was transported to a local hospital where he recovered. “The life-saving medal may be awarded to an employee, reserve, or volunteer who performs an exceptional act under emergency or extraordinary conditions in the furtherance of human life. It is clear that Officer Singh’s actions meet the criteria,” said Bowers. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved a few changes to their plans for a remodel of the Police Dispatch Center at the recent council meeting. The remodel is still going forward as planned with a few changes to ensure the center has an uninterrupted power supply. “We’ve identified some stuff where we couldn’t meet building code without making some amendments,” said Daniel Gonzales, Director of Public Works. “The amendment [of he plan] is about changing the location of a backup generator.” The Police Dispatch Center currently shares a backup generator with City Hall and the Fire Department. “If the power goes out, we have to prioritize Dispatch, which means shutting the other two down,” said Gonzales. “Energy security,” as he put it, is the city’s priority in the new plans. The main entrance to the Police Dispatch Center is not currently ADA-compliant, which will be corrected in these changes. Gonzales confirmed that there are plans to make sure dispatch services remain uninterrupted during the center’s remodel. “The plan is for dispatch to remain in place, build out the new space, make the new space operational, then cut over to the new dispatch, then decommission the old dispatch space.” At a recent City Council Meeting, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers confirmed that construction on the Dispatch Center is slated for early February 2024.
articles.title: City Council makes changes for Police Dispatch Center

articles.text: The 11th Annual Artisanal Brewing Competition will bring homebrewers from around the Bay Area to Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, October 6. The event which runs from 5:30- 7:30 p.m. will feature tastings from over 12 craft brewers, and an authentic Oktoberfest dinner on the front lawn provided by Piedmont Grocery. Admission to beer tasting includes a custom PCA beer glass for unlimited tastings of the brewers’ creations. Patrons can also enjoy the traditional Oktoberfest faire of freshly grilled bratwurst, potato salad and red cabbage – which can be enjoyed on the PCA lawn. Guests are encouraged to bring a picnic blanket to fully enjoy the warm fall weather and the lovely view of the sunset. This year’s talented brewers include Piedmont natives Zachary Jones, Carter Dunlap and Case Gardner vying for the bragging rights of Best Pale Ale, Lager, IPA and Best in Show. Talented brewers from the Bay Area Mashers Homebrew Club will be on hand looking to steal the show from the hometown favorites. Late entry and defending champion in the Lager and Porter Categories, Bob Davis of Happy Girl Brewing Co., will return this year with four new concoctions. Davis is excited to share a “Tastes Like Summer” Kolsch, a “Dead Man’s Hand” Black Double IPA, “Reflected Glory” a Trappist Tripel, and “Siren’s Song” a Black Pepper Saison. While the event is a celebration of brewing craftmanship, competition for the best beer in each class is steep. Determining the winners will be done by this year’s judges, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Piedmont Community Church Student Pastor Scott Kail, Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson and Piedmont City Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. Chad Olcott of Mulberry’s Market will be the festival’s first MC. articles.text: On Sunday, September 24, the Piedmont Center for the Arts hosted an early preview by artists who will be featured in this year’s Art Walk. Oil paintings tackled both abstract and hyperrealism as they lined the walls of the Center’s main gallery. “This is the first year that we’ve been able to put all the artwork into one place. You can get a little sense of everybody in the event,” said Jon Schleuning, lead organizer for the event. “Before, you could never see everything in one place, so it’s really great. If you want to preview to buy, that’s terrific, but it’s also great to just see the range of creativity in the community.” When it comes to creativity, Piedmont certainly has range. Several professional artists are featured in this year’s art walk, including Bonnie Bonner, Emily Keyishian, and Irene Nelson, whose art was accepted for the 2023 de Young Museum’s Open Exhibition. The de Young Open is the only exhibition of its kind at a major American museum. It invites local artists to submit their work and those few selected display their pieces in the de Young Museum’s Herbst Exhibition Galleries. Selected artists may offer these pieces for sale and retain 100% of the proceeds. Schleuning believes that Piedmonters can benefit from seeing the art at the preview exhibit at the Center for the Arts, even if they plan on going to the Art Walk on Sunday, October 1. “I think there’s huge value to that. People are visual, so if you see something that you like, that helps you know where you want to go during the event. It’s pretty spread out, so it just allows you to plan your day a little bit better,” he said. Twenty percent of all sales from the Art Walk will go toward supporting art programs in Piedmont schools. articles.text: Scouts from seven different Piedmont Girl Scout Troops helped clean up Crown Beach on Saturday. More than 40 girls from seven Piedmont Girl Scout Troops took part in the 39th Annual Coastal Cleanup Day on Saturday September 23, at locations around the Bay Area, including Crown Beach in Alameda and Shorebird Park at the Berkeley Marina. The girls ranged in age from 6 to 16 and consisted of four second grade brownie troops (30981, 31318, 31605 and 31370), 7th grade Cadette troop 33587, 8th grade Cadette troop 33521, and an 11th grade Ambassador Troop 33426. They joined more than 25,000 other volunteers throughout the state to remove 126,605 pounds of trash and an additional 7,041 pounds of recyclable materials – a total of 67 tons on its path into the ocean. Volunteers not only removed trash from the environment, but they also kept track of all the items they removed as part of one of the world’s largest and longest-running community science projects. This data, and the trends it displays over the many years in which it has been collected, has revealed a great deal about the extent and nature of the marine debris problem. It has provided California with crucial information needed to address the sources of the problem. Based on past cleanup data, 75 percent of the debris removed by volunteers was composed of plastic, a material that never completely degrades. Plastic debris can kill wildlife, leach toxic chemicals into the environment, and even introduce them into the food chain. The data has also shown that up to 80 percent of the trash on California’s coast originates on land, so volunteers across the state helped prevent enormous amounts of trash from reaching the ocean. Troops found the experience fun, interesting, educational, frustrating and even gross at times. Troop 33426 picked up 274 cigarette butts by way of example. pages.text: Wednesday, September 27, 2023 7 Piedmont Girl Scouts help on annual Coastal Cleanup Day Scouts from seven different Piedmont Girl Scout Troops helped clean up Crown Beach on Saturday. More than 40 girls from seven Piedmont Girl Scout Troops took part in the 39th Annual Coastal Cleanup Day on Saturday September 23, at locations around the Bay Area, including Crown Beach in Alameda and Shorebird Park at the Berkeley Marina. The girls ranged in age from 6 to 16 and consisted of four second grade brownie troops (30981, 31318, 31605 and 31370), 7th grade Cadette troop 33587, 8th grade Cadette troop 33521, and an 11th grade Ambassador Troop 33426. They joined more than 25,000 other volunteers throughout the state to remove 126,605 pounds of trash and an additional 7,041 pounds of recyclable materials – a total of 67 tons on its path into the ocean. Volunteers not only removed trash from the environment, but they also kept track of all the items they removed as part of one of the world’s largest and longest-running community science projects. This data, and the trends it displays over the many years in which it has been collected, has revealed a great deal about the extent and nature of the marine debris problem. It has provided California with crucial information needed to address the sources of the problem. Based on past cleanup data, 75 percent of the debris removed by volunteers was composed of plastic, a material that never completely degrades. Plastic debris can kill wildlife, leach toxic chemicals into the environment, and even introduce them into the food chain. The data has also shown that up to 80 percent of the trash on California’s coast originates on land, so volunteers across the state helped prevent enormous amounts of trash from reaching the ocean. Troops found the experience fun, interesting, educational, frustrating and even gross at times. Troop 33426 picked up 274 cigarette butts by way of example. The girls followed the cleanup with a picnic and treats for a funfilled and memorable day. Brownie Troop 31605 enjoyed observing a caterpillar and learning about swallowtail butterflies during the day. articles.text: Beach Elementary School parents started a new, more efficient, and safer way to drop kids off at school in the morning. From 8:15 to 8:30, every morning, the Linda Avenue side of the school near the play structure will be a drivethrough, drop-off only area. The new system is aimed at easing parking and traffic congestion and began on Monday, September 18. It will be staffed by parents for a few weeks. This replaces the previous loading zone and temporary parking during morning drop off. Parents are asked to not get out of their vehicles and to follow the traffic cones. “Drive-through drop-off at Beach is off to a terrific start thus far. It really does feel like it is accomplishing the intended purpose of enhancing student, parent, and staff safety by streamlining drop-off while helping alleviate parking plus traffic congestion around campus,” said Anant Ahuja, Chair of the Traffic and Safety Committee at Beach. The impetus for the change came from Beach School parents who noticed increasingly unsafe conditions during drop-off times. At the request of the Beach Parents Organization (BPO), and with the support from Principal Anne Valva, the Traffic and Safety Committee was formed to solve the issue. Along with Ahuja, Beach parents Zeena Fakoury, Liz Jobst and Brooke Wall round out the team that made the change. To prepare for Beach DriveThrough Drop-Off: • Do not get out of your car • Plan to have your kid(s) ready with backpack within reach • Children should be able to get out and close the door on their own • Once your kid(s) have been dropped off, pull out promptly to advance the line • Watch for bicycles • Do not block the crosswalk Parent volunteers Zeena Fakoury and Amy Vallerie help launch the new drive-through drop off on Monday, September 18.

articles.text: When I worked as an Account Executive for Yelp, my manager held a few team meetings where everyone went around and talked about what their purpose was and why. I was not very thrilled about the prospect of a career in sales at that point and I dismissed this “Finding Your Why” activity as just another dumb thing they made us do. Turns out I was completely wrong. After completing my Applied Positive Psychology program and becoming a Focus Coach, I learned that understanding the greater purpose behind why you’re doing the things you do is actually a key ingredient for happiness and success. I found out that our brains are actually wired to want to believe in something and people who do have something to believe in have a significant advantage over the people who don’t. Religion, spirituality, and values are all different examples of connecting to an overarching purpose for your life. For those who do not belong to an organized faith it can often be challenging to incorporate meaning, purpose, and belief into our lives. Two different experiences that everyone has access to are awe and transcendence. Awe is that lovely feeling you get when you look at a beautiful work of art or hear one of your favorite songs. Transcendent experiences are those moments where you feel inexplicably connected to the world around you; oftentimes these experiences occur in nature, in large gatherings of people such as concerts and protests, or in places of worship. These experiences give us a sense of being part of something that’s larger than ourselves and make us feel glad to be alive. As a coach I advise my clients to prioritize having more of these experiences to increase their overall wellbeing and to help them explore values, meaning, and purpose more deeply. Whether you consider yourself spiritual, religious, or secular, Positive Psychology research tells us that believing in something and understanding your purpose is a fundamental part of a truly happy and connected life. My coaching is very personalized to the needs of the client; I have some clients that love diving into this and others that prefer to focus more on achievement and engagement. I feel so lucky to be able to work with people on achieving more happiness and success in their lives and purpose is one of my favorite things to work on. Do you need help finding your why? articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. Eden on the road in Hayward 12-6 in come-frombehind fashion. “I can breathe now,” said coach Beth Black with a laugh. “It was a hard week because we were inside and had to cut practice short due to the smoke [from forest fires]. We did some good reps on Monday. The girls’ understood what they needed to do. When they were on the field, they executed. I loved it,” she added. The Highlanders scored all of their points in the second half, including the game-winning score on a 4th-and-goal play with just 15 seconds left. Quarterback Friedie Schickendanz found Malea Hartford with a nine-yard touchdown pass. On the play, Schickendanz began scanning the field to her right before rotating back to the left, rifling a pass to Hartford. It came on a play the team had recently installed in its the playbook earlier in the week, With smoke blanketing the area, the squad was forced to practice indoors during the week. “What’s fun about it was I wasn’t at practice the day we installed that play. And then the next day, practice got cut in half because of smoke. So I actually ran that play only once. I just took a deep breath and threw to the first open girl I saw. It was awesome,” said Schickendanz. “We just learned a new play in Tuesday’s practice; I basically just ran straight and sat right on the goal line. Friedie put in an amazing pass and we scored,” added Hartford. Piedmont’s first points in school history were scored earlier in the game by backup quarterback Peyton Watson, and made a 26-yard run, evading multiple tacklers on her way to the end zone. On a 3rd-and-5 situation Watson tucked the ball under her arm and juked past a tackler. Initially she thought her flag was pulled after feeling a tug at her jersey. But she heard her teammates telling her to run, so she burst into another sprint and followed blocks on her way to the end zone. “I was just running as fast as I could. I was checking for my flags once I reached the end zone [to make sure it hadn’t been pulled],” recalled Watson. Eden’s initial drive on 4th-and-goal at their own 16-yard line, driving the next possession to the Monarch’s 15 before the series stalled out. After forcing Mt. Eden to punt, Piedmont conceded the first points of the game after tossing a pick-six at their own 29-yard line to Monarchs’ linebacker Angelina Roxas, making it 6-0 after a failed two-point conversion with 4:10 left in the half. On a 4th-and-7 situation, Schickendanz hit #7 on a critical eight-yard pass for the first down at the 19-yard-line. After conceding the game’s opening touchdown, Piedmont went on to score 36 unanswered points with commanding “It was a tough week of practice [with the smoke], we only had one day on the field and the rest was just walk-throughs. It showed up early in the first half, but it was great to see the kids bounce back, work tough, and fight through it. To run off 36 straight points was great,” said coach Jordan Seiden. PHS’ win improves their record to 3-2 with three straight wins, holding their opponents to just one score in each of the victories over Arroyo, Encinal, and Mt. Eden—accumulating a point differential of 123-18 during the span. Piedmont’s defense, once again, was instrumental on Saturday afternoon, shutting down Arroyo’s heavy run set to force the Dons into uncomfortable passing situations. “We were going against some tough offensive linemen, but we were able to go in and make pressure. Our coach [Pouhila Tauaho], he helped us create slants and d-line stunts. We were able to get in the backfield and make the quarterback scared in the second half. We saw their size, so we just wanted to match up the gaps for gaps. Once we stopped the run, then we stunted their offense,” said defensive end Jordan Alemania. Linebacker Brandon Dicke had a huge day, recording a critical tackle for a loss on 4th-and-1 at the Dons’ own 30-yard line while the Highlanders held a onescore 16-8 lead. He also nabbed an interception on Arroyo’s last series. Dicke recalled the critical fourth-down stop. “Our play was called ‘lightning,’ which is where I blitz from the outside. It was a dive towards the middle A-gap. The defensive end on my side, Albert Bellingrath, rushed inside which freed up the outside for me. I got in there and made the tackle,” said Dicke. The game also featured a long 82-yard touchdown carry by quarterback Markos Lagios, outrunning the defense on a run straight down the middle of the field. “The o-line made that one. The offensive line made all their blocks, it was perfect. That’s what happens when we execute. I thought they’d catch me. They obviously had us in size on the line, but it showed our line can battle adversity,” said Lagios. articles.text: Piedmont claimed its first league win in a dominant 21-8 victory over San Leandro. Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team claimed a one-sided 21-8 win over San Leandro at the Pirates’ home pool on Tuesday, September 19. It was their first win against Western Alameda County Conference competition. It was an impressive performance Piedmont’s offense with a season-high 21 goals. Scored by 10 different players. Abigail Jacoby led with four goals, and Kat Melian and freshman Esme Krumins had 3-goal hat tricks.. “Kat is a really powerful shooter. We can have her score from different angles and long shots. Esme has been impressive, she has a lot of experience in the pool and it shows,” said first-year head coach Georgia Lewis. The Highlanders ended the first quarter with a 6-4 advantage and pushed the lead to 11-5 by halftime. PHS never let off of the gas pedal, putting in six goals and conceding twice in the third period to lead 17-7 entering the fourth. They added four more goals and allowing one in the final quarter. In the first period PHS opened quickly with three unanswered goals by Abigail Jacoby and two by leading scorer Melian within the first two minutes of the game. After a San Leandro goal, Melian got her hat trick with 3:03 left in the first. After a second SLHS goal, Olivia Kaltner made it 5-2 with 2:35 to go. Esme Krumins made it 6-3 with 1:41 left. Sage Gilbert made it 7-4 to start the second quarter with a goal near two minutes in, while successive goals by Melian, Anne Reardon, and Alicia Bernales made it 10-4 with 2:37 left in the first half. Jacoby scored her second goal with 20 seconds left in the half, making it 11-5. In the third, San Leandro made it 11-6 but Piedmont quickly responded with a goal from Gilbert at 5:34. The Pirates converted a 5-meter penalty, 12-7, but Piedmont then added four straight goals to end the quarter by Krumins, Kaltner, Jacoby, Vivian Burke—16-7. Sydney Olson scored the opening goal in the fourth, 17-7 after 40 seconds. Krumins got her hat trick with 4:32 left, making it 18-8, followed by the Highlanders scoring the game’s final three goals by Jacoby, Julia Montes, and Reardon. Final stats: Jacoby led the way with four goals. Melian and Krumins each had three goals. Reardon, Gilbert, and Kaltner finished with two goals apiece. Scoring individual goals included Burke, Olson, and Bernales. Tuesday vs. Berkeley Piedmont traveled to Berkeley on Tuesday, September 26 for another league match. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-4 overall, 1-1 league) travel to Newark Memorial today, September 27, for a 5:30 p.m. match. Our Sunday hike is a 6.7 mile loop along the Harkins Ridge Trail to Whitemore Gulch Trail, then back to the car. Starting on Harkins Ridge will start you going downhill with just around 230 feet in elevation gain for the first 3.5 miles. You’ll pass beneath groves of redwoods and get a brief glimpse of Purisima Creek. But after the creek and rightturn through a gate, your relaxation is just about over. Past the creek, you’ll gain over 300 feet in .3 of a mile and another 450 feet over the next mile. The final two miles of the trail back to the car will include over 900 feet in elevation gain, including a group of seven switchback turns that pick up near 400 feet in nearly a mile. In total, this 6.7 mile hike included over 1,600 feet in elevation gain. Although several sites list Harkins Ridge and Whittemore Gulch as “heavily trafficked trails,” I passed approximately 46 people during peak hours around 10:30 a.m.—calculating to fewer than seven people passed per mile. Punch in Purisima Creek North Ridge Trailhead to access this loop. Nearby is the South Parking Lot, which connects you to the historic Purisima Creek Trail, which has remnants of the logging mills from the early 1900s. articles.text: Clyne’s Wild Geese performed at Cabrillo Festival Music review by Paul Hertelendy The shortest was also the most memorable and newest at this year’s Cabrillo Music Festival in Santa Cruz: The six-minute world-premiere of Wild Geese by Anna Clyne as the season-finale number by the orchestra. What I admire most about the petite, soft-spoken English composer is her ability to engage the listener again and again – here at Cabrillo, August 13, heard for the seventh time (and still being streamed). The current radio play brings her once again to the forefront. Here, she leans in part on timeless past English styles, perceptible for nearly two centuries. She summons up a serene orchestral palette, with solo sonorities popping up here and there. The music is refined and restful, yet with good forward propulsion even in mundane gestures, like the cello section playing alone in unison. It’s a broadbased music, built on traditions of the past, offending no one, yet inevitably ear-drawing. With the help of audio engineer Jody Elff, the 43-yearold composer co-developed a marriage of live orchestra and computer-controlled processes without making it sound like electronic music – perhaps a promising future avenue. Wild Geese was written in inspiration from a poem by Mary Oliver. Music Director Cristian Macelaru led the unveiling. Yes, the innovation was of significance, with portends for the Foley proved to be an accomplished bass player himself, able to bring it out of the world of growls into the sunlight. Even longer was Pulitzer-Prize-winning Kevin Puts’ Concerto for Orchestra, also inspired by poetry, and notable for Puts’ great gift for incorporating fetching melodies. Dan Caputo’s Liminal dealt in hypnotic repetitions and fast runs up and down the scale. In addition to the tributes for Ellen Primack, so esteemed for her 33 years as festival executive director, attention was also devoted to the festival’s co-founder in 1963, Robert Hughes, who passed away last year at 89. The polymath bassoonist, conductor and composer was represented by his Estampie, which itself was a tribute to his predecessor composer and sometime mentor, Lou Harrison. Estampie, featured by both in revival moods, had been a pre-Renaissance dance form. articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy For our computer era, we get the ultimate lightning opera ideal for commuting city toilers in a perennial rush. All 20 scenes are pressed into 80 minutes of fast-flashing scenes, or four minutes PER average segment. You’re carried along as if riding the crest of a wave. Packed in are gigabytes of drama about the flawed genius of the handheld, a brainy superman with super weaknesses. If only he’d taken time to hold hands more often in his abbreviated life. The (R)evolution of Steve Jobs is a hit opera playing in eight cities in just six years at a pace comparable to Verdi. And now it’s come to the S.F. Opera, the city of Jobs’ birth. Created by the fast-rising local-turned-international composer Mason Bates, 46, it’s a bio-opera of the work-obsessed creator of the ubiquitous “device,” that magical iPhone that does nearly everything short of brushing your teeth. The college dropout Jobs (1955-2011) was the ultimate mercurial phone-computer geek, a classic Asberger’s case, both self-absorbed and ruthless as he was driven in developing his ingenious product designs reflecting miniaturization that no one had thought possible before. All the while driving partners, colleagues and ladies to distraction day and night in his frenetic drive. This candid biography of the abusive, workaholic wizard demands to be seen and heard. As A flawed hero, he belongs in opera, where we have encountered predecessors like Turandot, Don Giovanni, Pinkerton and Lady Macbeth. Flashing by like a supersonic missile and reeking with authoritarian venom, he marshals his employees and lady-loves like a Pied Piper, leading even himself toward an early grave. This work is powered foremost by baritone John Moore in the lean-and-mean title role, which fits him like a glove. The lady-loves are Chrisann (Olivia Smith), whom Jobs had impregnated then disavowed, then in the larger role, the spouse Laurene (mezzo Sasha Cooke), neither of them showing convincingly what made them fall in love with the cad. The strongest moments of the work come in scenes with Jobs’ spiritual adviser in matters Zen, Kobun. Here bass Wei Wu batBaritone John Moore sings the title role in Mason Bates’ opera, The (R)evolution of Steve Jobs, now in performance at San Francisco Opera. tles Jobs’ frenzy with some of the choicest interplay crafted by librettist Mark Campbell. Along the way comes tenor Bille Brulei as Wozniak, the partner pummeled by Jobs’ ire. The orchestra under the crisp guidance of Michael Christie played a lesser part with the scurrying of its augmented and electronic percussion, rising to the fore in two intense orchestral segments catching the drama. One ingenious facet of composer Bates was providing an identifying sonic identity to each of the major characters entering the scene. The opera chorus sang with tireless power, despite making more entrances and exits than in anything previous. The complexities of multiple scenes were managed by Stage Director Kevin Newbury. These smooth changes, with panels glowing in electronic circuitry, helped make this production much more effective than the one encountered at the New Mexico world premiere. ADDENDA – Born here of Syrian parents, Jobs’ name was originally Abdul Lateef Jandali….A techno artist emerged from the pit to take bows with the singers on September 24, receiving animated applause from an audience clearly captivated by his work. His name? Mason Bates, yes, the same….The most memorable music for these ears was Jobs’ “Tap, Tap” opening aria, the first-scene aria of Kobun, and the eulogy “Look Up” by Laurene with the chorus. articles.text: Over 20 pieces on display by the San Francisco-based artist An exhibition featuring 20 pieces of art by the late local artist Bernice “Bingo” Bing (1936- 1998) is now on view at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Born in San Francisco’s Chinatown in 1936, Bing was a young artist among the city’s Beat Era art scene, creating works from the 1950’s on. Although she grew up in an orphanage and bounced between foster homes as a child, she was able to earn her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the California School of Fine Arts, now the San Francisco Art Institute, where she studied alongside painter Elmer Bischoff and other greats. Her paintings and illustrations explore abstract expressionism and figuration to work as well as Zen calligraphy and Western abstraction. Bing only recently became recognized for her artworks, though she was a fixture in the San Francisco arts scene until her death in 1998. Into View: Bernice Bing is the first in an ongoing series of collection exhibitions at Asian Art Museum that highlight the work of under-recognized modern artists. It will be on view through June 26 next year. For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/into-view-bernicebing/. Artist Bernice Bing

articles.text: I Am Love (lo sono l’amore) has an all-star international cast of actors including Tilda Swinton. I Am Love (lo sono l’amore) is rich and sumptuous and endlessly interesting foreign film set in Italy. It also possesses an unexpected denouement. It is rich and sumptuous and an endlessly interesting. It also possesses an unexpected denouement. First things first: the film has a fine performance by a most gifted actresses, Tilda Swinton. Her career has been one of strong and nuanced roles, demonstrating a remarkable ability to convey complex emotions with a penetrating and even stoic expression, buttressed by an abiding sense of restraint. Some of her best work has been as a supporting actress. Swinton won an Oscar for her role as Karen Crowder in the 2008 film Michael Clayton. However, in films where she has the lead – The Deep End, and the strange and androgynous Orlando – she demonstrates a talent that astonishes, possessing depth and breadth in equal measure. Importantly, she has avoided creating a Hollywood persona of a glamorized actress. I Am Love is a project she long wished to bring to the screen. The film is a study in contrasts. Initially it is languid and studied, sorting out the Recchis, an extended, affluent Italian family who have issues and tensions. And then, suddenly, it’s a finale that almost requires a suspension of disbelief. The premise of the film is familiar: Emma (Tilda Swinton), a Russian émigré who married into a patrician Milanese family at a young age, has spent her life running a large household and staff, raising children, serving sumptuous, elegant dinners (she’s a fine cook), who now finds herself feeling a nudging ennui. The children are grown, her husband, Tancredi (Pippo Delbono), is enmeshed in his textile business, and the mansion, despite the presence of countless servants, seems empty. Emma’s mask of contentment and equanimity never appears false or stoic, so lavish and full is her life. And yet, as act two concludes, she opens like a flower, consumed by emotions. She is served a plate of prawns cooked by Antonio (Edoardo Gabbrielllini), a young chef and a friend of her son, Edo (Flavio Parenti). Emma steps into act three with an abandon (accompanied by an operatic score by John Adams) that telegraphs that this will not end well. What makes her decision to pursue a relationship with Antonio so jarring is that it seems so profoundly out of character. If Emma were a woman of deep, surging passions, repressed behind designer clothes and a stunning, elegant affluence, all while running her household and living a privileged life, then her fate would be comprehensible. However, not a hint is given. She is suddenly out of control, in the grip of a consuming, voracious carnality that morphs into a daytime soap opera. I Am Love is essentially a character study. Though histrionic in its final scenes, it is still, in a strange and disturbing way, compelling. As is Tilda Swinton. I Am Love (lo sono l’amore). Directed by Luca Guadagino. Starring Tilda Swinton, Marisa Berenson, Flavio Parenti, Edoardo Gabbriellini, Gabriele Ferzetti and Alba Rohrwacher. in Italian with English subtitles. 1 hr., 59 min. Rated R. Released in 2010. articles.text: Recall that women, coerced or not, accompanied their guy friends – boyfriends, spouses, movie buddies – to see Hangover, the surprise hit of 2009. It’s about a bachelor party in Las Vegas that soon bungee-jumps into disaster, with one set piece after the next, more outrageous and laugh-filled than the one before. Bridesmaids could be construed as women saying, “Oh yeah? Well, here’s our take on the pre-wedding rituals that lead up to the nuptials. If you want outrageous while abandoning all semblance of decorum, we’re going to bring it.” And the women of Bridesmaids (or better said, the writers Kristen Wiig and Annie Mumolo) don’t hold back. Let the meltdown begin. And there are scenes that are so brash and raunchy that it’s possible to laugh and cringe at the same time. But then Judd Apatow (Knocked Up, The 40-Year-Old Virgin) produced the film and, according to reports, couldn’t resist putting his oar in. Some say his screenplays are facsimiles of the backs of public bathroom stall doors. But perhaps that’s a bit harsh. Here’s the different between Bridesmaids and films of the Hangover ilk: the former has at its center a tender, insightful and raw character study. Kristen Wiig’s portrayal of Annie is wonderful. Wiig is not only a gifted comedienne, but also a superb actor. Annie is the designated maid of honor for her best friend forever, Lillian (Maya Rudolph). She is filled with joy and best wishes for her friend, though plagued by an abiding sense of angst regarding her own life. She’s adrift. Her one attempt at doing something for herself – opening a small bakery – was flattened by the recession. She’s recently lost her boyfriend and her sex-buddy, Ted (John Hamm), is a self-absorbed heel. She’s having an existential crisis while all about her swirls the intense chaos of pre-wedding planning. That’s the other interesting aspect to Bridesmaids: it deconstructs, in a sad, hilarious, sometimes crude way the rituals engaged in by women as they prepare one of their own for the moment when she is to be handed from her father to another man. There’s the selection of the bridesmaids’ gowns, the bridal gown, the shower, the wedding itself, and all attendant details. It all makes the women a bit crazy – led, of course, by Annie who is fully prepared to dive into the deep end of an empty pool. If the film has a flaw, it might be that it strives to surpass the guy flicks. It’s not a contest that this film should want to win. What Bridesmaids does, something that Hangover would never consider, is to possess a central character that is wounded and vulnerable, a woman on the verge. The writers believe, ultimately, in character, and develop the idea that sometimes life can seem to conspire not in the affirmative but in the negative. And then, happily, it doesn’t. Things once again begin to work out. As they do for Annie. Nice. At least for these two families. Bridesmaids. Directed by Paul Feig. Starring Kristen Wiig, Maya Rudolph, Rose Byrne, Jon Hamm, Melissa McCarthy and Chris O’Dowd. 2 hrs., 5 min. Rated R. Now streaming on VUDU/peacock/Netflix/Prime/ Apple tv A scene from Bridesmaids

articles.text: Jennifer Aniston and Owen Wilson star in Marley and Me Marley and Me has all the signs of a filler film. You know, one of those saccharine movies that’s as far from any reality being experienced by families today as Hollywood can make it. But then when it comes to depicting suburban life in America, surreal is often the screenwriter’s default position. Consistently, there is a glow about these films; they are usually much ado about nothing, and often leave the audience feeling a bit empty. Marley and Me tries for more and surprises. Though it’s billed as a film about a sweet, ever disobedient Golden Lab, it proves instead to be about a couple, Jenny (Jennifer Aniston) and John (Owen Wilson), who adopt an irresistible pup, Marley, and then, over the next 12 years, go on to have three children, transforming their lives. Marley is the sixth member of a family and though his antics often dominate, making for some comedic moments, he never overwhelms what turns out to be a nicely told story about the messiness and compromises involved in having children and keeping everything and everyone afloat. Marley, as it turns out, represents all those aspects of life that seem impossible to contain. Shirttails are always slightly un-tucked. Nothing is ever symmetrical. The surprises, the unexpected, the maddening feel of things being slightly out of control, the arguments and moments of sadness and disappointment are all wrapped up with Marley. The kids from age 10 and above will enjoy Marley and Me. There is much to be said for this lighthearted film. For anyone who has brought a dog into his or her life and has experienced the unconditional love offered each day by such a pet, well, Marley and Me is a must see. Marley and Me. Directed by David Frankel. Starring Jennifer Aniston, Owen Wilson and Eric Dane. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG. Released 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. T TH HE E

articles.text: I always assume that parents are in the hunt for a good PG movie. When I saw the trailer for Dolittle, it looked like a good prospect. It seemed to be a highend, glossy production with massive numbers of critters, all chattering away with the renowned Dr. John Dolittle, veterinarian, this time portrayed by Robert Downey Jr., a superb actor, no matter the iron suit. Most of what follows, however, amounts to a heads up for the parents. The story is loopy, with voiceover delivered by a parrot, Polynesia (Emma Thompson). And word is that the studio opened the budget spigot, spent months doing a reshoot and rewrite, and still ended up with a movie that kids will happily watch, but from an adult perspective, struggles for coherence. The movie begins with two kids (Harry Collete as Tommy and Carmel Laniado portraying Lady Rose) making their way to see Dr. D. for very different reasons. Tommy has a wounded squirrel, which he shot by accident. Lady Rose is there on behalf of Queen Victoria, who has fallen into a coma and is in need of medical attention, no matter, apparently, that Dr. D. is a vet. What they find is that the famous Dr. Dolittle has become a hermit in a walled-off ramshackle mansion due to a broken heart. We’re told by Polynesia that his much loved wife was lost at sea some seven years ago, hence his retreat from the world, comforted only by animals that talk in a manner only the doc can understand. The two kids, wandering through chaotic rooms, finally find the doctor, surrounded by a menagerie of animals, hiding Robert Downey Jr. in Dolittle (2020)

Craft brewers will present their favorite creations to share. Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson returns to provide a traditional German dinner of grilled bratwurst, red cabbage, and potato salad to enjoy on the front lawn, with live jazz by PHS musicians Will Kennedy, Alden Meil, and Ryan St John. Sunday, October 8, 11 a.m.– 2 p.m. Calif. Printmakers Art Exhibit Opening The California Society of Printmakers is a non-profit arts organization promoting the practice and appreciation of fine art contemporary printmaking, with the mission to both support the integrity of traditional printmaking and to provide a home for artists exploring new directions in contemporary print methods. CSP is the oldest print-making organization in the nation. Currently, the CSP has a membership of approximately 250 artists and though the majority of our members live and work in Northern California, membership is open to printmakers throughout the world. This, the 109th Annual Members’ Exhibit, will have Gallery Hours open to the public starting Sunday, October 8, and then Saturdays and Sundays through October 29, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. There will be an opening reception from 6–9 p.m. and no gallery hours on Saturday, October 14. Sunday, October 8, 5:30 p.m. In the Tradition Jazz & Pops Concert In the Tradition Piano Trio – Bill Jackman, Michael Jones, and Anthony Pegram – will perform a concert paying tribute to Jimmy Van Heusen, who composed nearly 1000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which 50 or more have become American standards. The concert is a benefit for Piedmont Center for the Arts and showcases its magnificent Steinway grand piano. Tickets $25 at the door, or $23 at https://bpt. me/5691334. Seating will be limited to the first 70 attendees. Sunday, October 15, 3:00 p.m. Piedmont Chamber Orchestra Fall Concert To celebrate Fall, the all-volunteer Piedmont Chamber Orchestra presents a concert, The Winds of Autumn, which includes the music of 18th and 19th century composers Johann Christian Bach, Franz Ignaz Danzi, and Johannes Brahms. The concert will feature wind instrument soloists, Marcelo Meira, clarinet, and Jeff Robinson, bassoon. A reception will follow. Admission is free and donations are gratefully accepted by this ProMusica ensemble, newly under the fiscal sponsorship of IntermusicSF.

articles.text: Italy is a diverse country in just about every way. Because of this, Italians should rejoice. They don’t, but we do in America. Salyards explained that Filoli’s team of horticulturists preserve the remaining ones by propagating, or growing new trees from Admission to the historic gardens at Filoli is included for all guests. original groves, using seeds, cuttings and other plant parts. “This orchard is about preserving this landscape feature of this estate. But we’re also trying to preserve some of the more rare heirloom varieties of fruit trees,” Salyards explained. Much of the bounty will be gone by the end of autumn. Guests will be invited to pick and taste fruit off the trees and enjoy table grapes from the harvest. Other apples, pears, plums and apricots will be churned into butters or liquified into ciders, which guests can enjoy under the shade of the trees in the walnut grove. Every Saturday through October 28, resident beekeepers will take guests to Filoli’s beehives where they can sample honey straight from the source. Filoli’s team expects one of their its biggest harvests this year, and nothing will go to waste. Village Harvest, a nonprofit volunteer organization that harvests fruit from backyards and orchards, will pick up the excess and bring it to food banks in the Bay Area. articles.text: As days grow shorter and leaves begin to fall, September is the ideal time to prepare for the colder months ahead. Avoid costly repairs and ensure your family stays cozy this winter with Honey Homes’ Fall Home Maintenance Checklist: 1. Inspect Gutters. Look for clogged downspouts. 2. Appraise the Roof. Keep an eye out for damaged areas or missing shingles. 3. Create a Patio Plan. Order covers for your outdoor furniture and grill now so they arrive before the rainy season. 4. Mind the Drafts. Inspect areas around windows and doors. Seal them up to keep cold air out and warm air in. 5. Check your Chimney. Do you use a fireplace or pellet stove? Schedule a chimney sweep and make sure the damper is working correctly. 6. Clean Dryer Vents. Lint buildup is a fire hazard! 7. Test Smoke & Carbon Monoxide Detectors. Replace batters when needed to ensure they are working correctly. 8. Change Air Filters. If you don’t remember the last time this happened, now is the perfect time ;) 9. Clean & Reverse Ceiling Fans: Dusting blades and reversing the direction of your fans helps distribute warm air more efficiently. 10. Inspect Faucets. Small drips now = big problems later. It suffices to say Scarecrow Alley was alive with creativity at Piedmont’s’ annual Harvest Festival in Piedmont Park. Kids in the community really took to this year’s theme, “Space Invasion,” with elaborate pop culture homages to Star Wars, Minecraft, and classic flying saucer mythology. As is tradition, each elementary school class in Piedmont has the opportunity to show off their creativity and create a scarecrow from scratch. These scarecrows are auctioned off to the community and the proceeds go to support the schools. “I think we have one from every single grade, except for maybe one,” said Poppy Crum, a volunteer parent organizer for Scarecrow Alley. “It’s a really awesome group that came together to make it happen between parents and kids.” And the results are equally awesome. Along the walkways in Piedmont Park were replicas of E.T., Marvin the Martian, dioramas of alien planets, and UFOs made from upcycled umbrellas. Scarecrows this year used a variety of different materials, from plastic to wood to metal and, of course, papier mache. In previous years parents brought the scarecrows to Piedmont Park. But this year, the volunteer team behind Scarecrow Alley Staff photos Nuala Price, 13, volunteers at the Kids’ Carnival with the classic game of knocking over a pyramid of cans with a bean bag. Beach School’s 4th grade class made what is easily the most unusual and one of the largest scarecrows ever made for the Harvest Festival, Jabba the Hutt, shown before and after being painted. provided pick up appointments via truck for the auction’s scarecrows. “The Makers community donated their truck; others have donated their trucks, sprinter vans, and their time to make sure these scarecrows come together,” said Crum. This action by the volunteers has made sure that barriers to entry are lower than ever. And a good thing too. “We’ve got some entries here this year that I don’t think would have gotten here without a flatbed truck,” laughed Crum. The Kids’ Carnival was equally lively this year as children flooded the parking lot above Community Hall, eager to grab a snow cone and play the different fairground-style games being offered. After grabbing a wristband or tickets at the carnival’s entrance, children spent the afternoon throwing footballs into nets labeled with different point values and knocking down aluminum cans with bean bags. Piedmont Real Estate Update September 2023 Rate Hikes End Eleven Years of Appreciation In 2022 and 2023, the Federal Reserve increased rates 11 times. As a result, these interest rate increases turned around 11 years of appreciation in East Bay cities that began in 2012. In Piedmont, when we look at sales data going back five years to January 2019, we see a steady upward appreciation trend until 2023. We do not yet have a full set of data for the current year; however, to date, homes in Piedmont appear to be selling on average for 10% less than they did at their average high sales price in 2022. Even with this, in Piedmont, we have seen an average annual appreciation of approximately 5% since 2019. In Oakland, we also see a steady upward appreciation trend until 2023. Like with Piedmont, we do not yet have a full set of data for this year; however, to date, homes in Oakland appear to be selling, on average, for 7% percent less in 2023 than they did at their average high sales price in 2022. Even with this, we have seen an average annual appreciation of approximately 4% in Oakland since 2019. In Berkeley, we continue see a steady upward appreciation trend line until 2023. It appears that for this year, Berkeley has seen average home prices drop nearly 13%, which is the largest drop of the three cities we are tracking. Piedmont Real Estate Update September 2023 Preparing for the New Season As summer winds down and we head into fall, spending some time on preventative maintenance for your home is essential. We may not need to worry about frozen pipes in the Bay Area – but rain, inefficient furnaces, and dirty fireplaces can all lead to unwelcome surprises. Please see the list below for some tips on protecting your property so you can enjoy a cozy winter season. If you need a referral for services, please reach out, or you can check caliahomes.com for our Homeowners Services Guide. Check your roof and clean rain gutters to avoid pooling water and leaks. Ensure no deficiencies exist in your home’s siding where water might enter. Consider using an air purifier as we tend to spend time indoors with windows closed during the cold months. Prune trees that may be at risk of falling during wind and rain. Have your fireplace and chimney inspected and cleaned. Check the batteries on your smoke alarms and CO detectors. Clean and cover patio furniture. Recaulk your windows to avoid heat loss. If you don’t already have a programmable thermostat, consider installing one. Smart thermostats are beneficial for efficient furnace use, saving on energy bills. Change the filter in the furnace. Spring isn’t the only time to clean; a general clean-up in and out is a good idea to prepare for fall and winter.
